optimization in non-stationary scenarios. Building on the soft actor-critic
algorithm, we modify its entropy model to incorporate temporal differences
and demonstrate that our approach can be extended to model-free reinforcement
learning frameworks, such as Q-learning. Theoretical analysis reveals that the
proposed algorithm ensures convergence of the policy gradient, even in non-stationary
environments, and numerical experiments confirm its effectiveness, also highlighting
its potential to handle non-stationary data samples. Additionally, the proposed
method is shown to be capable of achieving a global optimal policy in challenging
non-stationary reinforcement learning tasks. As an extension, we explore its
applicability to online learning and provide empirical results that show its
superiority over traditional methods in non-stationary settings. The accompanying
code is available for public access at https://github.com/stephentorn/NonStationary
Reinforcement Learning. Furthermore, a Python package named pyNSRL has been
released, providing a user-friendly interface for implementing the proposed
algorithms. In the future, we plan to expand the proposed method to encompass
multi-agent reinforcement learning scenarios. All accompanying materials, including
code and experiments, will be released at https://sites.google.com/view/turnover-reinforcement

Current video conferencing systems struggle with performance under poor network conditions. To address this issue, we introduce Confruce, a novel approach that combines efficient encoding and improved quality. Building on the success of SVC and HEVC, Confruce enhances the existing codec by incorporating a new motion vector block separation technique, which allows for better motion compensation even in damaged frames. Experimental results show that Confruce significantly improves video quality in low-bitrate scenarios, surpassing the capabilities of traditional video codecs. Our solution is already integrated into WebRTC and is available as an open source extension for web browsers and applications. To further evaluate its effectiveness, we created a comprehensive benchmark, YCVTE, which simulates real-world video conferencing scenarios and is accessible at https://ycvte.github.io. Using YCVTE, we demonstrate Confruce's superiority over existing codecs in real-world applications, achieving up to 7.5 dB improvement in video quality. Confruce is also being used in Google Chrome and is expected to become a standard part of future browser releases. Specifically, we demonstrate that a graded Lie-Rinehart algebra L, defined over a graded vector space A, can be expressed as the direct sum of its components L_(i), each dependent on the i-th power of a graded vector field, for all positive powers n. This result also implies that the graded algebra A, equipped with a finite-dimensional Lie-Rinehart algebra L, can be expressed as the direct sum of its components A_(i), for all positive powers i, provided L has a finite-dimensional basis. Additionally, we derive the corollary that if A is a graded algebra with a finite-dimensional basis, it can be expressed as the direct sum of its components A_(i), for all positive powers i, whenever L has a finite-dimensional basis. Moreover, we show that a graded Lie-Rinehart algebra L, defined over a graded vector field A, can be expressed as the direct sum of its components L_(i), for all positive powers i, provided the Lie-Rinehart algebra has a finite-dimensional basis. This result also implies that a graded algebra A, equipped with a finite-dimensional Lie-Rinehart algebra L, can be expressed as the direct sum of its components A_(i), for all positive powers i, whenever L has a finite-dimensional basis. Our proof is based on the graded Lie algebra of differential operators on the graded vector field A, which is a key tool for our direct sum decomposition theorems. Furthermore, it is shown to be more efficient than existing methods, achieving this efficiency on images with lower quality than those assumed by alternative frameworks. We investigate the evolution of an Efimov system of three bosons with a repulsive delta interaction at a universal strength, following a sudden quench from a scattering length to zero. Our calculations using the multichannel $k$-matrix approach reveal that this process generates a bound state of three bosons, known as an Efimov state, which then influences the system's dynamics. We find that the system's time-dependent wave function can be expressed as a combination of products of two-body wave functions and a state that is orthogonal to all two-body states. In real-world scenarios, machine learning models often encounter data they've never seen before. This is where open-set recognition comes in, a task that distinguishes between known (training set) and unknown data. Unlike closed-set approaches, which consider unknown data as a distinct class, open-set recognition provides more accurate predictions for known classes by taking the unknown into account as a separate entity. This paper introduces a novel deep learning model, Deep Open-set Information-theoretic Discriminator (DOID), which leverages the underlying structure of the data to improve open-set recognition. DOID combines two neural networks to generate two types of information: one highlighting the differences between known and unknown data, and the other capturing the underlying structure of the known data. By integrating these two signals, DOID makes predictions that outperform existing methods on various datasets. Notably, DOID's training process is efficient, requiring only a fraction of the time it takes to train existing models. This efficiency, combined with improved accuracy, makes DOID a promising solution for real-world applications. Experiments on multiple real-world datasets have confirmed the effectiveness of DOID.
